title: Drug-induced pigmentation (amiodarone, minocycline)
summary: Blue-grey, slate or brown discolouration caused by drugs such as amiodarone and minocycline, usually on sun-exposed skin or scars. Recognise it, review the drug and set expectations about slow fading.

glance.think: Blue-grey or slate discolouration of the face or sun-exposed skin in someone on long-term amiodarone or minocycline.
glance.engine: Drug or drug–melanin complexes deposited in the dermis, often worsened by UV light.
glance.backbone: Medication review with the prescriber (amiodarone is often essential); sun protection; explain fading takes months to years.
glance.never_miss: Other amiodarone toxicity (thyroid, liver, lung, eyes); Addison’s disease or haemochromatosis as non-drug causes.

list: **Amiodarone** causes two linked skin problems: **Phototoxicity** — burning/erythema within hours of sun exposure (UVA); up to 30–75% of patients; **Blue-grey (slate) pigmentation** of sun-exposed skin (~1–10%), usually after **months of treatment and high cumulative doses** (>40–160 g)
The case: a 50-year-old man in a sunny country, 3 months after starting amiodarone (dose recently increased), with increased sun sensitivity and a facial photo showing blue-grey discoloration.
Amiodarone and its metabolite **desethylamiodarone** absorb **UVA (300–400 nm)** and generate reactive oxygen species → phototoxic injury.

Both are **lipophilic**, with an extremely **long half-life (~50 days, range 20–100)**. They accumulate in dermal macrophages as **lipofuscin-like granules with drug–lipid complexes**, and melanin rises → blue-grey colour.

features: Burning, erythema and prickling minutes to hours after sun, even through glass (UVA). Later, **blue-grey/violaceous** colour of the **face (nose, cheeks), ears and backs of hands**. Also look for other amiodarone toxicity: thyroid (hypo-/hyperthyroidism), liver, lung (pneumonitis/fibrosis), eyes (corneal microdeposits, optic neuropathy), peripheral neuropathy.
diagnosis: Clinical (history + distribution). Biopsy only if doubtful (yellow-brown granules in macrophages; Fontana-Masson). Check **TFT, LFT**, CXR ± PFT, and arrange ophthalmology review per the amiodarone monitoring schedule (BNF: TFT/LFT every 6 months).

list: **Exogenous:** systemic drugs — phototoxic or photoallergic (see *Drug-induced photosensitivity — thiazide case*); topical agents — fragrances, sunscreens (photoallergic), **phytophotodermatitis** (psoralens in limes, figs, celery, giant hogweed), tar
**Idiopathic photodermatoses:** **polymorphic light eruption (PLE)**, actinic prurigo, **chronic actinic dermatitis**, solar urticaria, hydroa vacciniforme.
**Genetic:** xeroderma pigmentosum, albinism, Bloom, Cockayne and Rothmund–Thomson syndromes.

differentials: **Blue-grey pigmentation DDx:** **minocycline**, antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine — shins/palate), phenothiazines (chlorpromazine), tricyclics (imipramine), argyria (silver), chrysiasis (gold), ochronosis (hydroquinone), Addison's (brown, not blue — the [skin signs of systemic disease](condition:dermatomyositis) notes), haemochromatosis, cyanosis, methaemoglobinaemia (dapsone).

ol: **Do not stop amiodarone yourself.** Discuss with the **cardiologist** (dose reduction or an alternative antiarrhythmic, rate/rhythm strategy, ablation).
The BNF advises avoiding sun exposure **during treatment and for several months after stopping** (long half-life).

**Pigmentation** fades very slowly over months to years after stopping or reducing the dose, and may be permanent. Camouflage makeup; Q-switched/picosecond laser (specialist, private) for persistent cases.
**Monitoring:** TFT, LFT (6-monthly), annual eye check, CXR baseline. Yellow Card.

management: Blistering phototoxicity; new breathlessness/cough (pneumonitis); visual change (optic neuropathy); thyroid symptoms; jaundice.
Counselling, photoprotection, monitoring, liaison with cardiology, Yellow Card. Antiarrhythmic changes are specialist/shared-care decisions.
red_flags: New pigmentation on amiodarone: check **thyroid and liver function** and ask about breathlessness (amiodarone toxicity).
Generalised pigmentation with tiredness, weight loss or low blood pressure: exclude **Addison’s disease**.
pearls: "Amiodarone sensitivity **goes through window glass**" — UVA, so driving and office windows count.
Effects persist for months after stopping (half-life ~50 days), and the pigment for longer.
Counsel at the first supply — the BNF lists phototoxicity among the amiodarone counselling points.
